lines.text: Four break-glass accounts. The passwords are in an envelope, in a safe, in an office that closed last year.
Then they're either unusable or somebody else's. Which do you want to find out first?

items.prompt: The break-glass envelope is somewhere in storage. What do you do?
items.risk: An emergency nobody can get into — or an envelope in the wrong hands.
timeout: The accounts stay live, their passwords in a box somewhere.

hints.text: What makes a lost password harmless — and whose job is that?

options.label: Leave it — nobody's needed them in six years
options.result: The day someone does, nobody can get in. And whoever finds the box can.

options.label: Ask the closed office's facilities team where the safe's contents went — and tell Sabine that, found or not, the accounts should be reset into the vault under two-person control, her decision
options.result: “Boxed and sent to storage.” Three hundred boxes. Sabine resets all four that afternoon; the envelope becomes worthless paper.
options.consequence: Find it or make it worthless — through its owner.

options.label: Reset the four passwords yourself — you have admin
options.result: Sabine: “Now four emergency accounts have passwords only you know.”
options.consequence: Fixes one debt by creating another.
options.fail: Access and the vault are security's.

options.label: Search the three hundred boxes
options.result: A week of cardboard. The accounts stay live meanwhile.
options.consequence: Effort aimed at the wrong fix.

items.title: The envelope.
items.body: The closed office's move inventory says the safe's contents were boxed and sent to storage. Storage holds three hundred boxes from that office; none says ‘break-glass’. Four emergency admin accounts for the room platform are therefore useless to Fenwright in an emergency — and fully useful to whoever opens the right box. Sabine doesn't search. She resets all four into the vault the same afternoon: two people to open, an alarm on every use, a new password after each one.
items.label: Test: how many were usable — and why a lost envelope is a risk.

items.title: ‘safe contents · boxed · to storage’
items.body: The closed office's move inventory, line 214: ‘Safe — contents boxed, sent to storage.’ Storage has three hundred boxes from that office. None is labelled ‘break-glass’.

items.title: Two keys, too far apart
items.body: During the Cold War, the underground crews who controlled some of the most dangerous weapons ever built worked under a two-person rule: launching needed two officers to turn two keys at the same moment — and the keyholes were set so far apart that one person could not reach both. No single person, however trusted, could do the most dangerous thing alone. Break-glass accounts borrow the same idea on a much smaller scale.

items.title: Sixty doors, one key.
items.body: The second debt is bigger. svc-rooms is the account every room controller uses to read the booking calendar. It has admin rights on all sixty controllers — far more than reading a calendar needs — and the same password for six years, typed into every room's configuration. Change the password in the directory tonight and all sixty rooms lose their booking link at the same moment: a blast radius of 100%, on a Tuesday morning.
items.label: Test: the exposure — and the largest share one key reaches after the split.
**Order it:** retire a key that opens sixty rooms.

items.prompt: Who owns fixing svc-rooms — and how?
unknown: Which rooms use it for what
items.risk: A lockout of every room — or a key that opens every room for years.

options.consequence: A single point of failure running the retirement of a single point of failure.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #119 · AVERY'S LENS  Security debt is paid in stages, by its owner  Old keys and forgotten emergency accounts are debts that grow quietly. Security decides how to pay them; the architect maps every door the key opens and stages the change so no single night can lock everyone out.  Four emergency accounts sealed in an envelope nobody could find — and one password that opened all sixty rooms.

options.label: “Because it's your account and your vault. I know which rooms it touches; you decide how it changes.”
options.reply: Then we'll get on. Bring me the stages.

options.reply: Nobody's being blamed. We're paying a debt.

items.title: ‘scheduler login: svc-rooms’
items.body: One line in a room controller's configuration file: ‘scheduler login: svc-rooms / ••••••••’. The same line, with the same password, in all sixty rooms. It only ever needed to read the booking calendar.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Access debt grows quietly: emergency accounts whose passwords nobody can find, and service accounts with too much power and the same password for years. Security owns every account and the vault; the architect maps every door a key opens and stages the change — smaller keys with least privilege, lab first, one per region, the rest, checked each time — then the owner retires the old key on evidence. Break-glass accounts belong in the vault under two-person control, alarmed and rotated after every use.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Which password in your work hasn't changed since you arrived?
